chapter: The 1949 band, breakup and later years
title: The 1966 Chez and Basin Street East comeback
summary: Barnet tried out a big band at a bad Los Angeles club, then opened in New York with Clark Terry and Nat Pierce, the only act that got paid, with the union bending its rules.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: That place on Santa Monica, the --

Yeah, horrible. An awful joint. But the only reason I went in there at all was Basin Street wanted me back with the big band, and I wanted to go to New York one more time, and Clarke and I had a pact, and Nat Pierce, and we had talked about it. I said, "If I can get Basin Street we're going to do this and we'll do that." It

was all agreed. So I called them and I said, 'All right, I've got the deal set. Are you guys still ready to go?' 'Yeah.' So I wanted a place to reacclimate myself to being in front of a band, and The Chez presented that, the feeling of leading a band, and also the mechanics of it. Because you forget, you get away from it, you know, I had to learn my own arrangements over again, plus put a lot of new ones in, which I did. And we played there two weeks, and business was not good. But I took Willie Smith with me. That's the only guy I took from California. And the other guys were waiting in New York. Clarke and Nat have gotten all these guys together and we rehearsed and we opened, and the band -- it was a gasser. Like the union had a beef about something there, and the guy came in and heard the band -- Vincent Battali or something like that -- he said, 'Oh, I couldn't do anything to hurt this band.' He said -- and they actually figured out a way to circumvent their own law so they couldn't disturb the band, which I thought was very singular, because 802 is notoriously the hell with you.

But we were there four weeks, and we were the only ones in the show that got paid. The Four Aces were on there -- not the -- the Four Tops. They were on there. They got stiffed. And there was another gal in there that was one of the -- the outfit put her in there. She was a very

nice little girl but she didn't belong in this company, you know, but I presume -- whether she got paid or not was unimportant. It was the exposure they wanted. But they didn't get paid. But this guy that had that place, I went to him. I said, "Look, are you going to pay me?" I said, "I hear rumors of how the joint's going to fold after New Years." And business, we were doing good business there, but the joint hadn't been doing good business. And he looked at me and he said, "You'll get paid." And by God, I did. And I'm the only one. And Joe Glazer had handled the Four Tops, and they didn't get paid. I did.
